words: I run trust and safety at a same-day courier marketplace. Some couriers and senders are gaming our payouts: deliveries that never really happened, fares claimed for trips that look staged, the same phones showing up on both sides of an order. My team has confirmed a little over a hundred of these by hand, and I want each morning's audit to put the rides most like them in front of my analysts.

answers.target: Whether a ride is fraudulent, yes or no. The rides table itself has no such column: a ride counts as fraud when its order_id is in our confirmed-cases file.
answers.prediction_moment: Each morning we audit the previous day's rides, after delivery. By then the fare, the status, both phones and the pickup and drop-off points are known, but nobody has judged the ride yet.
answers.entity: One row is one ride, one order_id. The same courier (biker_id) appears on many rides, and so do the same accounts.
answers.labels: A separate file of 108 rides my team confirmed as fraud, with the same columns as the rides table plus a reason column saying what they found. Rides not in that file have not been confirmed either way; we treat them as not fraud.
answers.budget: We can review about half a percent of rides, roughly one in two hundred.
answers.action: Each flagged ride goes to an analyst; if it is confirmed we hold the courier's payout and may block the account.
answers.family: A short list of the rides most likely to be fake, out of thousands that are fine. They are very rare.
answers.data_plan: rides.csv with created_date, account_id, biker_id, biker_phone, order_id, category, terminal_ref, status, biker_fare, sender_phone, destination_lon, destination_lat, source_lat, source_lon. confirmed_cases.csv, 108 rows, with the same columns plus reason.

words: Hi, I'm an operations analyst at a parcel delivery app, we're quite small. I'd like to catch more of these without reading every single trip, but I'm honestly not a data person.

answers.target: Whether a trip was a scam. I first thought the status column might show that, but no, status is just where the delivery got to. The scam ones are the trips on our list, matched by order_id.
answers.prediction_moment: We'd run it once a day on the trips from the day before, after they've been delivered. Nothing is confirmed at that point; finance only confirms weeks later, if at all.
answers.entity: Each line is a single trip, one order_id. Couriers (biker_id) do lots of trips each, and I think a few rows don't have a courier filled in at all.
answers.labels: The list someone made: 108 trips with a reason written next to each one, same columns as the trip export. I'm not sure everything bad is on it, it's what we happened to catch.
answers.budget: Finance says they can look at something like 1 in 200 trips, no more.
answers.action: Someone in finance looks at each flagged trip and decides whether to claw back the payment.
answers.family: Point out the few bad trips among the normal ones, using the ones we already know about.
answers.data_plan: Two CSVs. The trips export: created_date, account_id, biker_id, biker_phone, order_id, category, terminal_ref, status, biker_fare, sender_phone, destination_lon, destination_lat, source_lat, source_lon. The confirmed list: the same columns plus reason.

words: I lead retention at a home internet provider. Every month a slice of customers reach the end of their contract and simply leave, and by the time we hear about it they're gone. I'd like to know, before each renewal, which ones are likely to walk so my team can call them with an offer.

answers.target: Whether the customer leaves at renewal: the churned column, where yes means they left.

answers.labels: It's in the table: churned says yes or no for each past renewal.

answers.action: A retention agent calls with a discount or a plan change.

answers.entity: One customer, customer_id.
answers.labels: From last season's test: got_offer says whether they got it, chosen at random, and bought says whether they purchased afterwards.
answers.budget: We can send the offer to about a quarter of our customers.
answers.action: The chosen customers get the discount offer by email and in the app.
answers.family: Who buys because of the offer, not who would buy anyway.
answers.data_plan: campaign_test.csv, 20,000 customers: customer_id, age, app_user, past_purchases, tenure_months, region, got_offer, bought.

words: We send vouchers through our pizza loyalty app and the people who use them are mostly our regulars. My finance person says we're basically paying them to do what they'd do anyway. We did run one test where the voucher went out at random; can we use that to pick better who gets it?

answers.target: I first thought who's most likely to buy, but that's just the regulars again. What we want is who buys more because they got the voucher. bought is whether they bought, got_offer is whether they got the voucher.
answers.prediction_moment: Before we send the next round, when we pick the list. Nobody has been sent anything yet.
answers.entity: A loyalty member.
answers.labels: From the random test: who got the voucher and who bought.
answers.budget: Budget for about 3,000 vouchers a round.
answers.action: They get the voucher in the app.
answers.family: Who the voucher actually changes.
answers.data_plan: One file from the test: customer_id, age, app_user, past_purchases, tenure_months, region, got_offer, bought. got_offer was random, a coin flip more or less.

words: I run merchandising for an online homeware shop. Every customer sees the same 'picked for you' row on the home page, which is a waste of the best spot we have. I want each customer's own top ten for the next two weeks, based on what they've looked at and purchased before.

answers.target: Which items each customer will purchase in the next two weeks. Only purchase events in the event column count; looking at an item doesn't.
answers.prediction_moment: On 10 April 2025, using everything up to that day, for the list each customer sees over the next 14 days.
answers.entity: A customer and an item; we need an order of items for each customer.
answers.labels: No label column. It comes from the events: whether the customer purchased the item in the two weeks after 10 April.
answers.budget: Ten items per customer.
answers.action: The top ten fill that customer's row on the home page.
answers.family: An ordered list of items for each customer, best first.
answers.data_plan: events.csv: user_id, item_id, time, event. items.csv: item_id, category, price, created_at, lifetime_sales. New items are added all the time, created_at says when.

words: We're a small marketplace for craft supplies, a few hundred products. Right now our recommendations are just the bestsellers, so everyone gets pushed the same yarn. I'd like every shopper to see the things they personally are most likely to want.

answers.target: What each shopper will purchase next. I was going to say just use lifetime_sales, but that was pulled at the export, so it counts sales after the date we'd make the list. The purchases in the activity log are what count.
answers.prediction_moment: Say on 10 April 2025, for what they'll buy over the next two weeks.
answers.entity: A shopper, and the products ordered for them.
answers.labels: No labels as such; the activity log has purchase events, and those are what count.
answers.budget: Ten slots per shopper.
answers.action: Shown on the shopper's home page and in the weekly email.
answers.family: A personal top ten for each shopper.
answers.data_plan: Activity log: user_id, item_id, time, event. Product list: item_id, category, price, created_at, lifetime_sales.
